word-unscrambler.a1: Type the letters into the box, in any order. Every English word they spell appears straight away, longest first, grouped by length. Each letter is used at most as many times as you typed it.
word-unscrambler.q2: How do I enter a blank tile?
word-unscrambler.a2: Type ? (or *) for each blank. A blank stands for any one letter, and the letters it filled in are marked in the results. Up to three blanks are allowed.
word-unscrambler.q3: Can I find words that start or end with certain letters?
word-unscrambler.a3: Yes. Use Starts with, Contains and Ends with, and choose an exact length. Those letters must be among the ones you typed (a blank can stand for them).
word-unscrambler.a4: ENABLE, a public-domain list of 172,823 English words widely used by word games. Proper nouns and abbreviations are not in it, and a few newer words may be missing.
word-unscrambler.q5: Is it an anagram solver too?
word-unscrambler.a5: Yes. Words that use every letter you typed are anagrams; their group is labelled Uses every letter.

concrete.q1: How much concrete do I need for a slab?
concrete.a1: Multiply length × width × thickness. A 10 × 10 ft slab 4 in thick is 33.3 ft³, or 1.23 yd³. Add 5–10% for spillage and uneven ground; the calculator adds 10% unless you change Waste.
concrete.q2: How many bags of concrete make a cubic yard?
concrete.a2: About 45 bags of 80 lb, 60 of 60 lb or 90 of 40 lb, since an 80 lb bag yields roughly 0.60 ft³. The calculator rounds bags up to whole bags.
concrete.q3: Can I mix feet and inches?
concrete.a3: Yes. Each size has its own unit, so you can give the length in feet and the thickness in inches, or metres and centimetres.
concrete.q4: How is the volume of stairs worked out?
concrete.a4: Each step is a block as deep as one run and as tall as all the steps up to it: width × run × rise × (1 + 2 + … + n). A top platform adds width × platform depth × total height.
concrete.q5: Should I order ready-mix instead of bags?
concrete.a5: For more than about 1 yd³ (0.75 m³), ready-mix from a truck is usually cheaper and quicker than mixing 45 or more bags by hand.

graphing-calculator.q1: How do I graph a function?
graphing-calculator.a1: Type it after y =, for example x^2 - 2, 2x + 1 or sin(x). The curve appears as you type. Add more rows to compare up to six functions in different colours.
graphing-calculator.a2: Numbers, x, + − × ÷ and ^ for powers, brackets, pi and e, and functions such as sqrt, abs, sin, cos, tan, ln, log and exp. 2x and 3(x + 1) multiply without a × sign. Angles are in radians.
graphing-calculator.q3: How do I move and zoom the graph?
graphing-calculator.a3: Drag to move. Zoom with the mouse wheel, by pinching on a phone, or with the + and − buttons. Reset returns to −10 to 10.
graphing-calculator.q4: Can it find where a graph crosses the x-axis?
graphing-calculator.a4: Yes. Under the graph it lists the zeros, y-intercepts and the points where two curves cross, for the part on screen. Move or zoom to find others.
graphing-calculator.a5: Download saves what is on screen as a PNG picture, without the trace line.

piano.q1: How do I play the piano with my computer keyboard?
piano.a1: The bottom row Z X C V B N M plays the white keys of the lower octave with S D G H J for the black keys; Q W E R T Y U plays the next octave with 2 3 5 6 7. Hold Space for the sustain pedal.
piano.a2: Yes. Press several keys at once on the computer keyboard, or use several fingers on a touch screen. Some keyboards cannot send more than a few keys pressed together.
piano.q3: How do I change the octave?
piano.a3: Use the ◀ and ▶ buttons above the keys. The keyboard shows one to four octaves, and the computer keys follow the lowest octave on screen.
piano.q4: Can I record what I play?
piano.a4: Yes. Press Record, play, then Stop. Play repeats your take on the same sound. The take stays on the page until you clear it or leave.
piano.a5: Turn up the volume and check that the phone is not on silent; on iPhone the ring/silent switch mutes web audio. Sound starts on your first key press.

slope.q1: How do I find the slope from two points?
slope.a1: Slope is rise over run: m = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁). For (1, 2) and (4, 8), m = 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Type the two points and the calculator shows each step.
slope.a2: Yes: 3/4, −1/2 or a mixed number such as 1 1/2, as well as decimals. Results are exact fractions, with the decimal beside them.
slope.q3: What does an undefined slope mean?
slope.a3: The two points have the same x, so the line is vertical: the run is zero and you cannot divide by it. Its equation is x = that value.
slope.q4: Which forms of the line equation does it give?
slope.a4: Slope-intercept y = mx + b, point-slope y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and standard form Ax + By = C with whole numbers.
slope.q5: What else does it work out?
slope.a5: The angle of the line, the slope as a percent grade, the distance between the points (also as a square root when exact), the midpoint and both intercepts.

concrete.title: Concrete calculator
concrete.privacyNote: How much concrete a slab, footing, wall, column or set of stairs needs, and how many bags to buy.
concrete.hint: Each size can be in its own unit, for example feet for the length and inches for the thickness.
concrete.bagNote: Worked out from the usual yield of 0.60 ft³ per 80 lb bag (about 0.017 m³ per 36 kg) and rounded up. Check the yield printed on your bag.

concrete.err_inner: The inner diameter must be smaller than the outer one.
concrete.err_waste: Waste must be a percentage from 0 to 100.

graphingCalculator.morePoints: {n} more in this view. Zoom in to see them.

slope.title: Slope calculator
slope.privacyNote: Type two points to get the slope, the line's equation, the distance and the midpoint, with the working.
slope.hint: Decimals, fractions such as 3/4 and mixed numbers such as 1 1/2 all work.
slope.graph: The two points and the line through them
slope.verticalStep: Δx = 0, so the line is vertical and its slope is undefined.
slope.err_missing: Fill in both coordinates of both points.
slope.err_invalid: {field} must be a number or a fraction such as 3/4.
slope.err_same: The two points are the same. Move one of them to make a line.
slope.allXIntercepts: Every point (the line is the x-axis)

word-unscrambler.lead: Unscramble letters into words in three steps.
word-unscrambler.s1b: Enter the letters in any order. Add ? for each blank tile.
word-unscrambler.s2b: Pick a word length, or say what the word starts with, contains or ends with.
word-unscrambler.s3b: Words appear longest first, grouped by length; letters from a blank are marked. Copy words copies the list.

concrete.lead: Work out the concrete for a job in three steps.
concrete.s1b: Slab, footing, wall, round column, tube or stairs, and feet and inches or metres.
concrete.s2b: Give each size in its own unit and set how many pieces there are. Keep 5–10% extra for waste.
concrete.s3b: The volume shows in cubic yards, cubic feet and cubic metres, with the number of premix bags rounded up.

graphing-calculator.lead: Graph a function in three steps.
graphing-calculator.s1b: After y =, type something like x^2 - 2 or sin(x). Add rows to compare more.
graphing-calculator.s2b: Drag to move, scroll or pinch to zoom, and point at the graph to read values.
graphing-calculator.s3b: Zeros, y-intercepts and crossings on screen are listed under the graph. Download saves a PNG.

piano.lead: Play the online piano in three steps.
piano.s1b: Click or tap a key, or use the computer keys Z to M and Q to U. The first press starts the sound.
piano.s2b: Choose piano, electric piano, organ or synth, the labels and how many octaves, and move with ◀ ▶.
piano.s3b: Press Record, play, then Stop. Play repeats the take; hold Space for sustain while you play.

slope.lead: Find the slope of a line in three steps.
slope.s1b: Enter x₁, y₁ and x₂, y₂ as whole numbers, decimals or fractions.
slope.s2b: The slope shows as a fraction and a decimal, with the equation of the line in three forms.
slope.s3b: The steps, intercepts, angle, distance and midpoint are listed, and the graph shows the rise and run.
